readings.title: The Little Girl with the Light
readings.challenge: Work out what the girl’s “light” is, since it is never a lamp or a candle.
readings.focus: Goodness and courage pictured as a light that changes how everyone else sees and acts.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. A maiden is a girl. To flee is to run away. A dell is a small valley in the woods. Tanglewood is thick, tangled undergrowth.
readings.contentNote: Enemies seize the palace and imprison the king and queen, and a lost child walks alone through a dark forest past hunters and wild animals that want to harm her. Nothing harms her, and her father finds her in the morning.

excerpt.locator: “The Little Girl with the Light,” the whole story without the motto for the mother printed before it; opens “There once lived a little maiden to whom God had given a wonderful light, which made her…”; closes “…creatures she gave love and protection, and she lived happily all the days of her life.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the girl’s light show? Find two places.
facilitatorNotes: In her smile as a baby, in her eyes like sunshine, and on her forehead like a star. The story repeats the sunshine-and-star words later, in the forest.
evidence: it lighted up her eyes like sunshine, and gleamed on her forehead like a star

questions.prompt: In the forest she sees a giant waiting by the path. What is it really, and what does her light change?
facilitatorNotes: Only a pine tree with “friendly arms.” Seeing clearly turns her fear into laughter, and the woods laugh with her.
evidence: it was only a pine tree, stretching out its friendly arms

questions.prompt: The rabbit will not come to the palace. Why does it want to go home, and why does she let it?
facilitatorNotes: Its babies are waiting and it has work to do. She loves it enough to let it go; caring for someone does not always mean keeping them.
evidence: My babies are waiting
So the child kissed it and bade it go

questions.prompt: What do you think the light stands for? Use something she does to explain.
facilitatorNotes: Kindness, goodness, courage or love are all defensible. Ask the child to tie the answer to an action: not being afraid, sheltering the rabbit, or ruling kindly when she grows up.
evidence: But she was not afraid,—no! not even when she came to a great forest, at evening;—for she carried her light with her.

readings.title: The Open Gate — out into the world
readings.challenge: Notice how the farm animals talk like neighbours, and find the first sign of trouble.
readings.focus: Freedom looks wonderful to the brown colt until it begins to hurt.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. A colt is a young horse. Brindle means brown with darker streaks. A threshing machine separates grain from straw, and the old steam ones had a loud whistle. Barbs are the sharp points on a wire fence.
readings.contentNote: The frightened colt jumps a barbed-wire fence and cuts himself.

excerpt.locator: “The Open Gate,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to the colt’s wish to see Dick; opens “One bright summer afternoon, Fleet, the good old shepherd dog that helped to take care of…”; closes “…and cut his feet as he leaped awkwardly over, "Oh! how I wish I could see Dick now."”.

questions.prompt: Before the trouble, what makes Fleet bark “with satisfaction”?
facilitatorNotes: Everything on the farm is in its place: hens in the dust, the calf asleep, ducks at the pond, horses at work. It is all calm.
evidence: so Fleet barked with satisfaction

questions.prompt: What do the three geese say has happened? How can you tell they are excited?
facilitatorNotes: The gate is open, the colt is gone, the calf is going, and they are “thinking about it”; they say it all in one breath and end with a honk.
evidence: The gate is open, the brown colt's gone, the brindle calf's going and we are thinking about it; quawk! quawk!

questions.prompt: Why does the colt shout “Hurrah!”? Does he know what it means?
facilitatorNotes: He copies Dick; he does not know the word, but he feels free and excited.
evidence: not because he knew what it meant but because he had heard Dick say it

questions.prompt: What changes the colt’s mind about being free?
facilitatorNotes: A loud whistle frightens him over a barbed fence; he tears his coat and cuts his feet, and wishes he could see Dick.
evidence: Oh! how I wish I could see Dick now.

readings.title: The Open Gate — the way home
readings.challenge: Find out who left the gate open, and notice how the boy and the colt are alike.
readings.focus: Carelessness has a cost, and both Dick and the colt come home changed.
readings.context: Recap: someone left the farmyard gate open, and the brown colt ran away. He loved his freedom until a loud whistle frightened him over a barbed-wire fence. Now the story goes back to the farm. A pike road is a main road. A cotton field grows cotton plants.

excerpt.locator: “The Open Gate,” from Dick at home to the end of the story; opens “But Dick was at home. He had run after the brown colt as fast as his feet could carry…”; closes “…them will ever forget the day when Dick was careless and did not shut the farmyard gate.”.

questions.prompt: Who left the gate open? What does Father say about it?
facilitatorNotes: Dick himself. Father says everyone, big or small, must take care of the things they want to keep.
evidence: for he was the very one who had forgotten to shut the farmyard gate
big boys and little boys and everybody else must take care of the things they wanted to keep

questions.prompt: Find two ways the colt and Dick are alike in this part of the story.
facilitatorNotes: Both hang their heads, and both think about each other all night. Both are sorry.
evidence: But the brown colt hung his head, as Dick had done

questions.prompt: The birds ask, “Is this the same brown colt that raised such a dust yesterday?” What do they mean?
facilitatorNotes: Yesterday he galloped proudly; today he limps home slowly. They notice how much he has changed.
evidence: Is this the same brown colt that raised such a dust yesterday?

questions.prompt: Dick and Fleet ask the colt no questions “because they understood.” What did they understand?
facilitatorNotes: That he was sorry and glad to be home, the way Dick was sorry. Some children may say they understood he was hurt; that fits too.
evidence: Dick and Friend Fleet asked no questions, because they understood

readings.title: The Giant Energy and the Fairy Skill — too strong to help
readings.challenge: Count the jobs the good woman gives the giant, and what goes wrong each time.
readings.focus: A giant who badly wants to help keeps spoiling things, and a patient friend shows him where to learn.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Energy means strength and the wish to keep doing things; skill means knowing how to do something well. A steeple is the tall pointed top of a church. Zeal is great eagerness. A cistern is a tank that holds water, and a pump brings the water up. A mullein is a tall weed with a long stalk.

excerpt.locator: “The Giant Energy and the Fairy Skill,” without the motto for the mother printed before it, from the start to the giant seeing the fairy palace; opens “Long, long ago, when there were giants to be seen, as they might be seen now if we only…”; closes “…pebbles, he heard a strange bird singing, and saw among the trees the fairy palace.”.

questions.prompt: Why will nobody give the giant work?
facilitatorNotes: He is so big and clumsy that he breaks things, like knocking down the steeple or tearing off part of a roof.
evidence: he was so great and clumsy that people were afraid to trust their work to him

questions.prompt: What three jobs does the good woman give him? What goes wrong each time?
facilitatorNotes: He carries china and breaks it all, runs with milk and spills every drop, and pumps water until the yard floods.
evidence: every bit of the china was broken
found her yard as well as her tubs full of water

questions.prompt: The good woman never scolds the giant. Why does she keep trusting him?
facilitatorNotes: She forgives him and loves him; she can see he truly wants to help. Some children will think she should give up; ask what would have happened then.
evidence: She had forgiven him for breaking her china, and had made up her mind to trust him again

questions.prompt: “Don’t go so fast. Stand still and listen!” Why are these just the right words for this giant?
facilitatorNotes: His trouble is always rushing and using too much strength; the directions only work if he slows down and notices small things, like a bent stalk and shining pebbles.
evidence: Don't go so fast,
Stand still and listen!

readings.title: The Giant Energy and the Fairy Skill — learning to be a helper
readings.challenge: Listen for each new thing the giant learns, and which part of the way home goes into his work.
readings.focus: Patient practice turns a clumsy giant into a maker of beautiful things, and he brings them home.
readings.context: Recap: Giant Energy, very strong and very eager, kept breaking and spilling whatever he tried to do, though a good woman kept trusting him. She sent him to learn from the Fairy Skill, through a meadow of daffodils, past a bent mullein stalk and a willow, and across a brook on shining pebbles. A loom is a frame for weaving cloth or carpet; a shuttle carries the thread under and over. A potter’s wheel spins so clay can be shaped into cups. A goldsmith makes things of gold.

excerpt.locator: “The Giant Energy and the Fairy Skill,” from the fairy palace to the end; opens “He never could tell how it looked; but he thought it was made of sunshine, with the…”; closes “And this is the way that young Giant Energy learned to be a helper in the world.”.

questions.prompt: What is the giant’s first job in the workshop? What does Fairy Skill do with her wand?
facilitatorNotes: Untangling threads without breaking them. Each time she makes them tangled again, so he must practise until it is perfect.
evidence: she changed them into a tangled heap again

questions.prompt: What things does the giant learn to make?
facilitatorNotes: Untangled threads, carpets on a loom, cups and saucers on the potter’s wheel, and chains, bracelets and necklaces of gold.
evidence: the giant learned to be steady

questions.prompt: His carpet looks like a meadow full of daffodils, and the pearls are like the brook’s pebbles. Why does he put those things in his work?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks of the way he came, which he learned by going slowly and noticing. Some children will say he is thinking of the good woman; the way led from her house.
evidence: As he wove, he thought of the way by which he had come

questions.prompt: Who gets the carpet, the cup and the chain? Why her?
facilitatorNotes: The good woman, the one he loves best, who trusted him when no one else would.
evidence: he hung the chain around the good woman's neck, and she was more beautiful than a queen

readings.title: The Search for a Good Child — Part 1: Five knights and Florimond
readings.challenge: Remember each knight’s name and what it means, and listen for what the knights care about most.
readings.focus: A king sends five good knights to find a good child, and the first “wonderful” child they meet is not one.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Knights were soldiers on horseback who served a king and promised to be brave and good. A king’s court is the place where he lives with his helpers. Plumes are feathers on helmets, and to draw rein is to stop a horse. A baron and baroness are a lord and lady who own a castle. Pure means good and clean in heart, and true means honest and loyal.

excerpt.locator: “The Search for a Good Child,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to the knights leaving the Baron’s castle; opens “Long, long ago there lived, in a kingdom far away, five knights who were so good and so…”; closes “…when they left him; but the knights did not care to stay with a child who was not good.”.

questions.prompt: What are the five knights called, and what does each name tell you?
facilitatorNotes: Brian the Brave, Gerald the Glad, Kenneth the Kind, Percival the Pure and Tristram the True. Each name tells his best quality. Help the child hear that each name begins with the same sound twice.
evidence: each one was known by a name that meant something beautiful

questions.prompt: What kind of child does the king want, and why?
facilitatorNotes: A good child, to live at court and learn to be a knight; he says a good child is worth more than a kingdom. Notice “if he will come willingly.”
evidence: Only a good child can be chosen. A good child is worth more than a kingdom.

questions.prompt: Many parents send messages praising their children. Why don’t the knights hurry to see them?
facilitatorNotes: The parents say their sons are beautiful or smart, but the knights care only whether a child is good.
evidence: as the knights cared nothing for a child who was not good

questions.prompt: Puff says Florimond is the most wonderful child in the world. What do the knights find out, and why do they leave?
facilitatorNotes: He is merry at first, but next morning he roars “Boo-hoo-hoo-hoo” because it is raining and he wants to play outdoors, and nobody can quiet him. Being handsome and clever is not the same as being good. Some children may feel a little sorry for him; ask whether everyone has bad mornings.
evidence: because the rain was coming down, when he wanted to play out of doors!

readings.title: The Search for a Good Child — Part 2: Little Gauvain
readings.challenge: Watch what little Gauvain does before he helps the knight, and why.
readings.focus: Sir Tristram meets a boy who keeps his promises, and sees what kind of child he is at home.
readings.context: Recap: an old king sent five knights, Brian the Brave, Gerald the Glad, Kenneth the Kind, Percival the Pure and Tristram the True, to find a good child to bring up at his court. Their first visit, to a rich boy named Florimond, ended when he screamed because it was raining. “Greeting to you” means hello. A comrade is a friend who shares your work. A fawn is a young deer.
readings.contentNote: Gauvain’s father died fighting in the king’s wars when Gauvain was a baby.

excerpt.locator: “The Search for a Good Child,” from the knights parting at the oak tree to Sir Tristram’s night at Gauvain’s home; opens “The knights began to think that their mission was a difficult one; but they rode on,…”; closes “…scarcely wait for the time to come when he should meet his comrades under the oak tree.”.

questions.prompt: What do the knights ask at every house, and how does their search go?
facilitatorNotes: “Is there a good boy here?” They are disappointed many times, so at last they part to search alone.
evidence: Is there a good boy here?

questions.prompt: Gauvain wants to help the knight. Why does he make him wait first?
facilitatorNotes: He promised to bring sticks and water to Granny Slowsteps before sunset, and he keeps his promise though he would rather help the knight.
evidence: for I promised to be there before the setting of the sun

questions.prompt: How do the animals and Gauvain’s mother greet him when he comes home? What does that tell you?
facilitatorNotes: The dog runs out, the cat rubs against him, and his mother calls him her sunbeam. He is loved at home, and he loves them back.
evidence: Is that my sunbeam coming home to roost?

questions.prompt: What does Sir Tristram notice about Gauvain at home? Which of these things would be hardest for you?
facilitatorNotes: He comes when called, feeds the cat and dog after his own supper, and goes to bed without fretting even while the knight is telling of lions and battles. Many children will say going to bed in the middle of a lion story is hardest. Ask why such small things show goodness.
evidence: went to bed when he was told, without fretting

readings.title: The Search for a Good Child — Part 3: Gauvain the Good
readings.challenge: Listen to each knight’s story and work out who the child is before the knights do.
readings.focus: Five knights have found the same good child, and his mother’s answer surprises them.
readings.context: Recap: an old king sent five knights to find a good child to bring up at his court. Sir Tristram the True spent a night at the home of little Gauvain, who kept his promise to old Granny Slowsteps and was loving and good at home with his mother. Now the knights meet again under the oak tree. To torment is to hurt or tease cruelly. To tarry is to stay. A clown here is a rough, rude fellow. Knighted means made a knight.
readings.contentNote: Rough men try to hurt a small dog, and a boy rescues it.

excerpt.locator: “The Search for a Good Child,” from the knights meeting under the oak tree to the end of the story; opens “"I have found a child whom you must see," he said, as soon as they came together.”; closes “…true. And he was beloved by all the people in the world, but most of all by his mother.”.

questions.prompt: What did each of the other four knights see or hear? Who was it every time?
facilitatorNotes: Gerald heard a boy singing under a heavy load; Brian saw a boy save a dog from rough men; Kenneth heard about the boy who helps Granny Slowsteps; Percival saw a boy wait patiently when the water was muddied. Every time it was Gauvain.
evidence: a little boy ran up, as brave as a knight, and took the dog in his arms

questions.prompt: Brian the Brave saw Gauvain being brave, and Percival the Pure saw him keep his temper. Why do you think each knight noticed what he did?
facilitatorNotes: Each noticed the goodness that matches his own name, perhaps because it is what he cares about most. Put together, they show that Gauvain has all five.
evidence: he spoke no angry words, and waited patiently till the water was clear again

questions.prompt: Why does Gauvain’s mother say no to the king? Is she right?
facilitatorNotes: She loves him more than a thousand kingdoms and cannot spare him. Some children will think Gauvain missed a great chance; others that home is where he belongs. The king himself agrees with her.
evidence: he is dearer to me than a thousand kingdoms

questions.prompt: The knights ride home sad, but the king rejoices. Why?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that such a child with such a mother will grow into a knight at home, and he is right: Gauvain the Good comes to his court in the end.
evidence: Such a child, with such a mother, will grow into a knight at home.

readings.title: The Closing Door — Part 1: The goblin comes in
readings.challenge: Notice the one door that is always open, and what the goblin says about calling Mother.
readings.focus: Little Daughter’s white room is full of treasures, and a strange visitor asks her to keep him secret.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. This is a picture-story: the room, the pearls and the door stand for something more, and listeners can wonder what. Swan’s down is a swan’s softest feathers. A goblin is a mischievous little creature of fairy tales. A playfellow is a playmate. To bid is to tell or ask.

excerpt.locator: “The Closing Door,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to the goblin’s first visit; opens “There was once a little girl (her best and sweetest name was Little Daughter), who had a…”; closes “…of fine lace for her darling, did not dream that a goblin was in the little white room.”.

questions.prompt: What is Little Daughter’s room like? Find words that make it white and shining.
facilitatorNotes: A snowy floor, a ceiling like a fleecy cloud, curtains like lily petals, a bed like swan’s down, white pansies and a dove.
evidence: it was white and shining from the snowy floor to the ceiling

questions.prompt: Where do her pearls come from, and what must she do with them?
facilitatorNotes: The king gives her a new one every morning, and she must keep them fair, ready to wear when he sends for her.
evidence: a new pearl was given her as soon as she waked up each morning
who bade her keep them fair

questions.prompt: Which door is always open? What does Little Daughter do when her mother calls?
facilitatorNotes: The door into her mother’s room. She always runs out at the first call and jumps into her mother’s arms.
evidence: there was one door which was always open, and that was the one which led into her mother's room

questions.prompt: Why does the goblin tell her not to call her mother? What do you think will happen?
facilitatorNotes: He says they are having a nice time and her mother is busy; really he does not want her mother to see him, or the room changing. Children may predict trouble, since the room is already growing like him. Ask whether a playmate who asks you to keep him secret from your mother is a good friend.
evidence: Oh! no; we are having such a nice time together, and she's busy, you know.

readings.title: The Closing Door — Part 2: The pearl turns dark
readings.challenge: Watch what happens to the room, the dove and the pearl, and what the goblin wants Little Daughter to do.
readings.focus: A darkened pearl and a creaking door bring Little Daughter running back to her mother.
readings.context: Recap: Little Daughter had a shining white room full of treasures, and a string of pearls from the king, one for every morning, to keep fair. The door to her mother’s room was always open. One day a goblin as black as coal came in to play and told her not to call her mother, and the room began to look more like him. Dingy means dull and dirty, and smutty means sooty. Hinges are the metal joints a door swings on. Fair here means clean and white.

excerpt.locator: “The Closing Door,” from the goblin’s tiptoeing to the end of the story; opens “The goblin did not make any noise, you know, for he tip-toed all the time, as if he were…”; closes “…put two golden hearts against it and nothing in this world could have shut it then.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to the room while the goblin plays? Why doesn’t Little Daughter notice?
facilitatorNotes: The curtains grow dingy, the floor dusty, the ceiling like a rain cloud; the pansies droop and the dove moans. The goblin amuses her so much that she does not see.
evidence: he amused the little girl so much that she did not notice the change in her dear room

questions.prompt: What happens to the last pearl, and what does the goblin say about it?
facilitatorNotes: It grows dark when he touches it. He says they can wash it, and asks what one pearl matters.
evidence: what difference does it make about one pearl?

questions.prompt: Why does the goblin want the door shut? What makes the mother look up?
facilitatorNotes: So that the mother will not see. The door has been open so long that it creaks, and the creak tells the mother something is wrong; she fears it might never open again.
evidence: it creaked on its hinges as the little girl tried to close it

questions.prompt: The pearl stays “a little blue always.” Why do you think the story keeps that one mark? What might the open door stand for?
facilitatorNotes: Some wrongs can be mostly mended but leave a mark, so it is better to call for help early. The door may stand for telling your mother, or whoever loves you, everything; accept other readings tied to the text, such as trust or love. The golden hearts keep it open.
evidence: except for the one pearl which was a little blue always
put two golden hearts against it

readings.title: The Minstrel’s Song — Part 1: The wind’s song
readings.challenge: Notice what the other minstrels talk about, and what Harmonius does instead.
readings.focus: Minstrels hurry to the king’s court, and only Harmonius stops to listen.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Minstrels were singers who travelled about long ago, playing the harp and telling stories in song. Heralds carried a king’s messages and blew trumpets to announce them. May-day is the first of May, a spring holiday. A cot is a little cottage. “Thee” is an old word for “you,” and “ye” means “you” said to many people. The chorus is the part of a song that comes back again and again.

excerpt.locator: “The Minstrel’s Song,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to Harmonius learning the wind’s song; opens “Once, long, long ago, there lived in a country over the sea a king called René, who…”; closes “…reached his friends, who were still talking of the grand sights that they were to see.”.

questions.prompt: Why does King René send for all the minstrels?
facilitatorNotes: To please Queen Imogen, who wants to hear them; every morning he asks how he can please her.
evidence: What can I do to please thee to-day?

questions.prompt: Why was everyone so glad when the minstrels came, long ago?
facilitatorNotes: There were no story books, so minstrels brought songs of knights, battles, hunters, fairies and goblins.
evidence: because there were no story books in those days

questions.prompt: What do the oldest and the youngest minstrels say they will sing about? What does Harmonius do while they talk?
facilitatorNotes: Drums and battles; ladies and their fair faces. Harmonius gathers wild flowers and whispers “Listen! listen!”
evidence: I can sing of the drums and battles
Listen! listen!

questions.prompt: The others hear “nothing but the wind.” What does Harmonius hear in it?
facilitatorNotes: A song of the wind’s travels over the sea, the hills and the valleys, with a chorus. Say the chorus together. Some children will say the others could have heard it too if they had stopped.
evidence: Nobody follows me where I go,

readings.title: The Minstrel’s Song — Part 2: Three singers
readings.challenge: Count the singers Harmonius listens to, and see who at court can name them.
readings.focus: Harmonius’s song from the wind, the brook and the bird wins the court, and the queen knows where it came from.
readings.context: Recap: King René called all the minstrels of his land to sing for his new queen, Imogen, on May-day. On the way, the other minstrels talked of the grand sights they would see, but young Harmonius stopped to listen and learned the wind’s song. Comrades are friends travelling together. A court is a king’s palace and the people in it. Mad here means out of his mind.

excerpt.locator: “The Minstrel’s Song,” from the minstrels walking on through the wood to the end of the story; opens “"We shall see the king and speak to him," said the oldest minstrel.”; closes “…it when I was a little child; and I can name the singers three." And so she did. Can you?”.

questions.prompt: What two other songs does Harmonius stop to hear? What do the others say each time?
facilitatorNotes: The brook’s and a bird’s. They say it is “only” a brook and “only” a bird, and hurry on to the king’s court.
evidence: Oh! that is only the sound of the brook trickling over the stones.
Oh! that is only a bird!

questions.prompt: What is Queen Imogen thinking of while the minstrels sing?
facilitatorNotes: Her old home and the butterflies she chased as a little child; she is a little homesick.
evidence: the queen thought of her old home, and of the butterflies she had chased when she was a little child

questions.prompt: How does Harmonius’s song sound? Why does it please the king and queen more than the others?
facilitatorNotes: Like wind, roaring sea and creaking trees, then a trickling brook, then all the birds in spring. Nobody had sung that before, and it brings back the queen’s childhood. Some children will say the others only sang what everyone already sings about.
evidence: It was as if you heard all the birds in Spring.

questions.prompt: The story ends, “Can you?” Who were the three singers, and why could the other minstrels not hear them?
facilitatorNotes: The wind, the brook and the bird. The others were too busy talking about the king, the crown and the jewels to listen. Ask what the child might hear outside if they stopped to listen.
evidence: Three singers sang along our way,
And so she did. Can you?

readings.title: Dust under the Rug — Part 1: Twelve little dwarfs
readings.challenge: Watch what Minnie does when she finds the messy little house, before she knows whose it is.
readings.focus: A girl sets out to earn money for her sick mother and becomes housekeeper to twelve dwarfs.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Diligently means carefully and hard. “As neat as a new pin” means very neat. A carpenter’s rule is a folding measuring stick, about two feet long. Dwarfs here are tiny fairy-tale people who keep gold inside a mountain. To sup is to eat supper. A mortal is an ordinary person, not a fairy, and a maiden is a girl. To prove faithful is to show you can be trusted.
readings.contentNote: The girls’ father has died, their mother falls ill, and Minnie walks alone through the forest at nightfall to find work. The story calls her sister lame, an old word for someone who cannot walk easily.

excerpt.locator: “Dust under the Rug,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to the last day of the fairy housekeeper’s holiday; opens “There was once a mother, who had two little daughters; and, as her husband was dead and…”; closes “…every day Minnie worked faithfully until the last day of the fairy housekeeper's holiday.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Minnie leave home, and why does her sister stay behind?
facilitatorNotes: Their mother is sick, it is winter, and they need food, so Minnie goes to find work. Her sister cannot walk easily, so she sews at home.
evidence: I must go out to find work, before the food gives out.

questions.prompt: What does Minnie find in the little house, and what does she do before anyone comes home?
facilitatorNotes: Twelve tumbled beds, twelve dirty plates and a floor so dusty you could draw on it. She warms her hands and then tidies everything.
evidence: the floor of the room so dusty that I am sure you could have drawn a picture on it
this will never do!

questions.prompt: How do the dwarfs talk? Say one of their rhymes together.
facilitatorNotes: All together, and in rhyme. Children can join in: “Now isn’t this a sweet surprise? We really can’t believe our eyes!”
evidence: for they always spoke together and in rhyme

questions.prompt: What do the dwarfs ask Minnie, and what do they promise? Why do you think they choose her?
facilitatorNotes: To stay through their fairy housekeeper’s holiday; if she proves faithful and good, they will reward her. They have seen her clean their house without being asked and wash up after supper.
evidence: Dear mortal maiden will you stay
And if you faithful prove, and good,

readings.title: Dust under the Rug — Part 2: The little voice
readings.challenge: Listen to what the stars say and what the little voice says, and notice which one Minnie cannot bear.
readings.focus: Minnie skips one hidden job, and her own heart will not let her rest until it is done.
readings.context: Recap: Minnie went out to earn money for her sick mother and her sister, and found a tiny, untidy house in the forest that belonged to twelve dwarfs who keep gold in the mountain. She made it clean and bright, and they asked her to keep house faithfully until their fairy housekeeper came back from her holiday. In winter, frost makes pictures on window panes. Pinnacles are the pointed tops of towers. A groat was a small old coin worth very little. A duty is a job you ought to do.

excerpt.locator: “Dust under the Rug,” from the picture on the window pane to the end of the story; opens “That morning, as Minnie looked out of the window to watch the dwarfs go to their work,…”; closes “…never forgot their lesson, to do her work faithfully; and she always swept under the rug.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Minnie late with her work on the last day?
facilitatorNotes: A beautiful frost picture of fairy palaces on the window; she gazes at it until the clock strikes twelve.
evidence: she forgot that there was work to be done, until the cuckoo clock on the mantel struck twelve

questions.prompt: What does Minnie tell herself when she skips sweeping under the rug? Is she right?
facilitatorNotes: That dust nobody can see does not matter. The story says it does, because she knows it is there. Some children will say it is only a little dust; let them argue it.
evidence: After all, it is nothing for dust to be where it can't be seen!

questions.prompt: The stars and the little voice in Minnie’s heart take turns. What does each one say, and why can’t Minnie bear it?
facilitatorNotes: The stars praise her as faithful and good; the voice says “Dust under the rug!” She knows the praise is not quite true, which makes her feel worse. Read the turns aloud in two voices.
evidence: There is the little girl who is so faithful and good
Dust under the rug! dust under the rug!

questions.prompt: What would Minnie have earned if she had left the rug unturned? What do the dwarfs want her to remember?
facilitatorNotes: Only a groat instead of twelve gold pieces. Even the smallest job done well brings joy. Some children will notice that she is rewarded for going back and finishing, not for being perfect.
evidence: A groat was all you would have earned.
That in the smallest duty done

readings.title: The King’s Birthday
readings.challenge: Follow Carl from the country to the city and into the church, and notice how he looks after himself.
readings.focus: A little boy lost in the king’s birthday crowd finds a gentler King in a church window.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Brindle means brown with darker streaks, and a mooley cow is one without horns. A steeple is a church’s tall, pointed tower. To trudge is to walk on and on when tired. Pillars are tall posts that hold up a roof. The windows like picture books are stained glass, pictures made of coloured glass. The Good Man with a lamb in His arms is Jesus, shown as the Good Shepherd, and in the Christmas story Mary is His mother.
readings.contentNote: Carl is separated from his mother in a crowd and is lost and alone for hours before she finds him.

excerpt.locator: “The King’s Birthday,” the whole story without the motto for the mother printed before it; opens “Little Carl and his mother came from their home in the country one sweet summer day,…”; closes “And in all the joy of the king's birth day, there was no joy so great as theirs.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Carl bring flowers to the city, and what happens to them?
facilitatorNotes: To throw before the king. They are trampled under the horses’ feet and the king does not care: the first sad moment of the day.
evidence: they were trampled under the horses' feet and the king didn't care

questions.prompt: How does Carl get lost, and what does he do when he is alone?
facilitatorNotes: Tired, his hot little hand slips from his mother’s and the crowd carries him away. He cries, then remembers it is the king’s birthday, wipes his tears and walks on. Talk about what a lost child should do today, such as staying put or asking a safe grown-up.
evidence: his little hot hand slipped from his mother's and he was carried away in the crowd
so he wiped the tears away as he trudged along

questions.prompt: Carl sees two kings that day. How are they different?
facilitatorNotes: The king on the gray horse rides by and does not notice the flowers; the Good Man in the window has a loving face and holds a lamb, and in Carl’s dream carries him to his mother. The story seems to say the second is the truer king. Some children will simply prefer the horse and the parade.
evidence: a dear, gentle Man, with a loving face, and He had a lamb in His arms

questions.prompt: What does Carl dream, and how does the dream come true?
facilitatorNotes: That a king with the Good Man’s face carries him to his mother; he wakes to hear his mother praying for him and runs to her. Some children will say the prayer was answered; others that his mother searched until she found him. Both can be held.
evidence: who was carrying Carl in His arms instead of a lamb, and was taking him to his mother
Mother! mother! here am I!

readings.title: The Story of Gretchen
readings.challenge: Notice who in this story is far from home, and who helps a stranger feel at home.
readings.focus: A homesick German girl in a new country decides nobody there keeps Christmas, until a kind stranger finds her empty shoes on Christmas Eve.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. Gretchen and her parents have just come from Germany to live in the United States. In Germany children set out their shoes before Christmas for Saint Nicholas or his helper, here called Rupert, to fill. A boarding-house rents rooms to people who eat together; a stoop is the steps in front of a door; a mission church helps poor people; jostled means bumped and pushed; carols are Christmas songs.
readings.contentNote: In the toy store Lindsay calls the Japanese dolls “funny slant-eyed dolls,” an old and hurtful way to describe people’s eyes; if a child notices, say so plainly.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of Gretchen,” the whole story without the motto for the mother printed before it; opens “It was almost Christmas time when one of the white ships that sail across the sea brought…”; closes “…a gladsome Christmas To all our fellowmen, Carol, brothers, carol! Christmas Day again."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Gretchen decide that people in America do not keep Christmas?
facilitatorNotes: Her father is ill, there will be no tree, and when she sets her wooden shoes outside the door they are never filled; people stumble over them and scold.
evidence: people stumbled over them and scolded
she decided that the people in America did not keep Christmas

questions.prompt: In the toy store, which toy does Gretchen love, and why that one rather than the fine princess doll?
facilitatorNotes: A plain baby doll that looks as if it wants to be loved. She is lonely herself, so the doll that needs love is the one that calls to her.
evidence: a look on its face as if it wanted to be loved
little mothers are the same all the world over

questions.prompt: How does Margaret know what the empty shoes on the stoop mean, and what does she give?
facilitatorNotes: She and her papa have been to Germany and know about setting out shoes. She lays her own baby doll, one that looks as if it wants to be loved, across them.
evidence: they had been in Germany, and they knew that the little owner was waiting
laid it tenderly across the wooden shoes

questions.prompt: Margaret and her papa run away before Gretchen sees them. Why might they do that? What makes Gretchen “feel at home” at last?
facilitatorNotes: They want the gift to come like Saint Nicholas’s, with no one to thank. The doll matters, but so does knowing that someone in this new land understood her. Children may also remember the poor woman who took Gretchen to the toy store: there are two kind strangers in the story.
evidence: for they had run away
made her feel at home
